title: Bears Lose TE Cole Kmet for Season After Patriots Injury, Coach Ben Johnson Confirms.
body:
Chicago’s offense will have to adjust quickly after tight end Cole Kmet was ruled out for the remainder of the season following a right‑knee injury sustained in the fourth quarter of Thursday night’s loss to the New England Patriots. Head coach Matt Eberflus confirmed the severity of the damage in a press conference, saying the team’s medical staff determined that Kmet’s injury will keep him sidelined for the balance of the campaign.

The 25‑year‑old Kmet, who entered the league as a third‑round pick in 2020, has been a reliable target for quarterback Justin Fields, finishing the season with 46 receptions for 447 yards and three touchdowns. His versatility—able to line up on the line, in the slot or out wide—has been a key component of the Bears’ evolving passing attack. Losing him not only deprives the offense of a dependable safety valve but also forces the coaching staff to reshuffle its tight‑end depth chart, likely elevating second‑string Nathan Peterman and rookie Jalen Cox to larger roles.

Kmet’s injury came at a critical juncture. The Bears, sitting at 3‑5, are battling to stay within striking distance of a playoff berth in a fiercely competitive NFC North. The Patriots, already out of contention, were still able to exploit Chicago’s defensive lapses, and a late‑game drive that saw Fields scramble and eventually throw a short pass to Kmet was halted when the tight end planted his right foot and felt an immediate pop. Initial scans suggested a possible ligament sprain, but an MRI later confirmed a torn medial collateral ligament (MCL) that will require a prolonged rehabilitation period.

The loss underscores a broader issue that has plagued Chicago this season: depth injuries at skill positions. Earlier in the year, the Bears lost wide receiver Dazz Lloyd to a hamstring strain, and more recently, running back Khalil Mack suffered a high‑ankle sprain that limited his effectiveness. Coach Eberflus, who previously coached high school football in the Chicago suburbs, acknowledged the challenge of maintaining continuity amid a spate of setbacks. “We’ve got to trust the guys who are stepping up,” he said. “Cole’s work ethic and preparation have set a standard, and we’ll carry that forward.”

Analysts note that the Bears’ offensive scheme will need to adapt without Kmet’s size and route‑running finesse. In the short term, the team may lean more heavily on the emerging partnership between Fields and wideout Darnell Mooney, while also incorporating more screen passes to the backfield to compensate for the reduced tight‑end presence. Defensive coordinator Sean McDermott will also have to consider adjustments on special teams, where Kmet has contributed as a blocker on punts and kickoffs.

Looking ahead, the Bears face a crucial stretch of games against divisional rivals Detroit, Green Bay and Minnesota. While the loss of Kmet is a significant blow, the organization’s depth chart suggests that younger players will receive valuable reps that could pay dividends in the long term. The front office is expected to explore free‑agency options to bolster the tight‑end position before the offseason, signaling that Chicago intends to address the roster gap rather than simply endure it. For now, the Bears must rally around the remaining veterans, adapt their play‑calling, and hope that the rest of the season unfolds without further major injuries.
